newsitem.title: USA: WHEAT -- US exporters facing aggressive competition.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT -- US exporters facing aggressive competition.

text.p: U.S. wheat exporters will have to be more aggressive to entice world grain buyers now that good harvests are set in Canada and the European Union as well as Australia and Argentina, wheat industry sources said.

The world wheat market has been a seller's market for months as global stocks fell to the lowest in decades early this year and prices hit all-time highs as worries about weather and disease in the U.S. crop rattled markets.
But all that has changed, as not only U.S. production but yields in its export competitors, have come in strong.

"That situation is 180 degrees different this year because Australia has a huge crop, Canada has a huge crop, Europe has a huge crop and Argentina has a good crop," a prominent U.S. exporter said. "There is a lot of wheat out there."

On Wednesday the U.S. Agriculture Department raised its estimate for 1996 U.S. wheat output by 47 million bushels from last month, to 2.296 million bushels versus 2.186 million in 1995. But it also dropped projected 1996/97 (July/June) exports to 925 million bushels from 975 million seen last month and a total 1.241 billion bushels in the 1995/96 season.
End-stocks projections for July 1997, were raised to 506 million bushels, up 97 million.

USDA pegged 1996/97 Canadian wheat production at 29.80 million tonnes, up from 25.43 million tonnes in 1995/96, Argentine wheat output at 14.00 million tonnes against 8.60 million tonnes a year earlier, and Australian production at 19.50 million tonnes, up from 16.98 million in 1995/96.

A second U.S. exporter said: "Right now, I would label this as a buyer's market. Whoever has the best price will get the sale. Our wheat prices are going down. That would spark some buying if prices are low enough."
The first exporter said the United States has to lose $25 a tonne on the flat price of its wheat in general.
"Argentinian wheat is trading down to a equivalent of $150 a tonne right now, and U.S. hard red winter wheat is around $170-$175 a tonne," the exporter said.

A third trader at a U.S. export firm agreed. "The bottom line is lower prices," he said, adding that Canada is now harvesting wheat and by December the Argentine and Australian supplies will be in the pipeline.
China, a major importer, also has a better crop this year, making the export pie that much harder to slice.
"We're going to have more competitive wheat markets next year," USDA Secretary Dan Glickman told reporters Wednesday.

Glickman also warned that the United States stands ready to renew its export subsidy battle with the European Union if the EU drops its recent export taxes and begins subsidizing sales to North Africa and other traditional customers.

Such sales years ago sparked creation of the U.S. Export Enhancement Program (EEP), which paid exporters the difference between world and domestic prices to achieve sales and was a lightning rod for trade arguments until its suspension last year.
"If they use export subsidies, we will aggressively use the tools at our disposal to fight fire with fire," Glickman told reporters in response to questions on Wednesday.
Alain Moulinier, head of France's grain office ONIC, said on Wednesday that European grain export subsidies are likely.
"Currently, we have taxes but we will return to subsidies," Moulinier said. "This does not mean we will need large subsidies to export."
"If the EU starts granting subsidies to capture export demand, I don't know if the U.S. can afford to stand idly by and not follow suit," one exporter said.
(Chicago newsdesk 312 408 8720)
